source: YouGov, 'Perceptions of how tax is spent differ widely from reality' (Nov 2014); Ipsos MORI / Royal Statistical Society / King's College London, 'Perceptions are not reality' (2013); TUC / YouGov welfare poll (2012)
note: The letter_guess allocations are YouGov's Nov 2014 mean responses when people were asked to divide their own income tax and NI across the Treasury's 15 tax-statement categories; actuals that year were the 2013-14 letter shares. The fraud and unemployment rows in guesses are measured against the benefits bill, not total spending. YouGov's Nov 2025 ranking study finds the public now over-rank debt interest and aid and under-rank pensions and education.

aid.factoid: The average guess in the last survey to ask for a number (YouGov, 2014) was £5 of every £100 of income tax. And when Ipsos asked in 2013, more people picked overseas aid as a top item of government spending than picked pensions, which cost nine times as much.

beliefs.text: Asked how much of every welfare pound goes to the unemployed, the average guess was 41p. The audited figure at the time was 3p.
Jobseeker's Allowance costs £0.3bn a year. The state pension costs £136.6bn, over four hundred times as much.
The public's average guess for benefit money claimed fraudulently: 24p in the pound. The official estimate: 0.7p.
Interest on the national debt takes £1 of every £12 the state spends: £106bn a year, up from £25bn as recently as 2020-21.
The average guess for spending sent to the EU was 7% while Britain was a member. The audited figure was about 1%. It is now 0.1%, residual withdrawal payments.
Overseas aid takes 0.7p of every pound the government spends: less than a penny, and less than a tenth of the interest on the national debt.
